name: Diego Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a big phosphate mine. Load at the shovel, drive up the ramp, tip at the crusher or the waste dump, back down, again and again, about thirty loads a shift. Eighteen months in. Before that I was twelve years an army cook and then a few years driving delivery vans.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father was a miner, coal, underground, and I always said I'd never do it. Then the delivery company started using route software that had us running like rats, and the mine paid better, so here I am. I'm still slow on the ramp in the wet and I take the corners too wide, my trainer Luis tells me every week. But I like it, it's honest, and I'm home most nights for dinner with Rosa and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market sorted it out, like it usually does. Companies tried it, it didn't pay, so they stopped. I'd probably say that at the barbecue and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, good. I'd get a few years to get properly good at the truck and maybe move to the dozer. My father did thirty years in one mine, and I'd like a bit of that steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, finish my training, try for the dozer ticket in a year or two. Keep putting a bit away, we're at about four months. And keep doing the odd barbecue catering job on weekends, which I do for fun and a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the route software at the delivery company. How did that feel at the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being watched by something that didn't care if you needed the toilet. It cut the time per drop and added stops until you couldn't breathe. That's partly why I'm cautious about all of this, even the boring version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the catering.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Army cook, so I can feed a hundred people out of a trailer. I do christenings, footy club days, the odd wedding. Rosa does the bookings and I do the smoke.

S0.say: I'd say the market sorted it out like it usually does: companies tried it, it didn't pay, so they stopped.
S0.think: I think it's good news: a few years to get properly good on the truck and maybe move to the dozer, with some of my father's steadiness.
S0.do: Keeps driving and finishes his training, aiming for the dozer ticket within a year or two. Keeps saving at about four months and runs weekend barbecue catering for extra cash.
S0.quote: Like being watched by something that didn't care if you needed the toilet.
S0.fieldNote: Diego reads the plateau through free-market eyes: if it doesn't pay, it stops. His memory of route software at the delivery company makes him wary even here. His army cooking has already become a small weekend catering business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get off the couch and learn something, and companies should run proper apprenticeships, not just hire from overseas or buy robots. A man should be able to learn a trade at any age. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the trucks would go first, because driverless haul trucks are already running at big mines. Junior drivers like me would be the first moved off. But a steady change gives me time to get into something else on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen a couple of the drivers move across into the workshop and do well, I'd apply for an adult heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine. I'd use the AI app now and then to help me with the theory, like I do now to plan fishing trips. And we'd pause the plan to buy a bigger boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in over the hills, you can see it but it's not here yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame the companies for chasing a better way, that's what business does. I'd blame people who wouldn't adapt, and governments that tie up apprenticeships in red tape. My old man retrained twice and never complained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see others move first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the army you learn not to be the first one through a door you haven't checked. Let a couple go through, see what happens, then follow. That's not fear, that's sense.

S1.say: I'd say people need to learn something new and companies should run proper apprenticeships, because a man should be able to learn a trade at any age.
S1.think: I think the trucks would go first and junior drivers like me would be moved off. But steady change gives me time to get into something else on site.
S1.do: Applies for an adult heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship once he sees colleagues succeed in the workshop. Uses an AI app now and then for theory and pauses plans for a bigger boat.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in over the hills.
S1.quote: In the army you learn not to be the first one through a door you haven't checked.
S1.fieldNote: Diego doesn't blame companies for automating; he blames red tape and people who won't adapt. His caution is framed as army sense, not fear. He has a concrete on-site path: an adult diesel fitting apprenticeship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and towns first. Local businesses, local churches, local people. I'd be wary of the government promising to fix it, but I'd want them to back apprenticeships for whatever's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm finished at the mine within a year. A fitter apprenticeship takes four years and there's no point starting if robots fix the trucks too. I've got four months saved and a mortgage. That's not much rope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, sell the boat and stop the private health extras. I'd grow the catering into a real business, because people will still want a man cooking at their daughter's wedding, I think. And I'd talk to Rosa about whether we hold off on moving Lucas to the private high school next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being dropped in the bush without a map. Alarmed, I'd say, and short-tempered at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't take the long road, only the short one. The short road for me is the barbecue trailer. With more years I'd have taken the trade and the trailer both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be wary of government. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes, but I'd want it as a bridge, not a bed. I'd rather it paid for training or helped small businesses start than just a cheque every fortnight.

S2.say: I'd say we need to look after our own, families and towns first, and be wary of government promising to fix it, though it should back apprenticeships.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished at the mine within a year, and a four-year apprenticeship is pointless if robots fix the trucks too. Four months saved and a mortgage isn't much rope.
S2.do: Cuts back hard, sells the boat and drops private health extras. Grows the catering into a real business and reconsiders moving his son to a private high school.
S2.feel: Alarmed and short-tempered, like being dropped in the bush without a map.
S2.quote: I'd want it as a bridge, not a bed.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI removes Diego's long road and leaves the catering trailer as his short one. He accepts government help only as a bridge, true to his views. He admits it would make him short-tempered at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a man to learn a new trade if he gets going. Companies and communities should make that easy. I'd tell the younger guys not to sit around waiting for someone to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is tight but workable. I could get most of a trade done, or build up the catering properly. I'd probably try both and see which holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first six months to see if the workshop is hiring adult apprentices. If it is, I'd go in. On the side I'd buy a second-hand cool room trailer for the catering, about eight thousand, and book more weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doing both a trade and the catering, with two kids, is a lot. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fishing, mostly. And Rosa would carry more of the bookings and the school runs. We'd talk about it at the kitchen table first, that's how we do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lucas a man works with what he's given. Carmen's seven, she'd just want to help with the barbecue, and I'd let her.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a man to learn a new trade if he gets going, and younger workers shouldn't wait for someone to fix it.
S3.think: I think five years is tight but workable for most of a trade or a proper catering business. I'd probably try both and see which holds.
S3.do: Watches for six months, then joins an adult apprenticeship if the workshop is hiring. Buys a second-hand cool room trailer for about eight thousand and books more catering weekends.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, and busy helps.
S3.quote: I'd tell Lucas a man works with what he's given.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Diego run two tracks at once, a trade and a growing catering business. He'd pay for it with his own leisure and more help from his wife. He makes big decisions at the kitchen table with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a fair go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, no excuses. Learn a trade, start a business, look after your family. That's what my father would've said too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright. Ten years is a whole apprenticeship and then some, and the kids would be mostly grown. I'd be fifty-three with a trade and a catering business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or so to see how the first adult apprentices do, then start mine. I'd keep the catering going on weekends and slowly build it up. We'd keep saving and pay a bit extra on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because robots could still fix trucks by then. But I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that worries you more than the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people get lazy. Ten years sounds like forever, so everyone puts it off. I've seen it in the army, you get a long warning and people still pack the night before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could tell the mine one thing, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give us a real apprenticeship pathway, not a brochure. And stick to it when times get tight.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, no excuses: learn a trade, start a business and look after your family.
S4.think: I think I'd be alright with a whole apprenticeship possible and the kids mostly grown. I'd be fifty-three with a trade and a catering business.
S4.do: Waits about a year to watch the first adult apprentices, then starts his own. Builds the weekend catering slowly while saving and paying extra on the mortgage.
S4.feel: Uneasy, since robots may still fix trucks by then, but able to sleep.
S4.quote: You get a long warning and people still pack the night before.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Diego's plan becomes a full trade plus a business. His main worry is people, himself included, putting it off. He wants the mine to commit to a real apprenticeship pathway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a real apprenticeship pathway funded by the companies, and help for small businesses starting out, not just cheques. Let people work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe pride. A lot of men around here measure themselves by their work. My father did, and I do too. Take that away and you've got more than a money problem.

headlineQuote: Take that away and you've got more than a money problem.
portrait: Diego Lopez is 43 and drives a haul truck at a phosphate mine, 18 months in after twelve years as an army cook and a stint driving delivery vans. He's traditional and free-market, doesn't blame companies for automating, and wants apprenticeships rather than handouts. He waits for proof before moving, an army habit. In Steady Disruption he plans an adult diesel fitting apprenticeship, under fast AGI he falls back on his weekend barbecue catering, and with more time he runs both.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it takes away the long road of learning a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A real apprenticeship pathway funded by companies, and help for small businesses starting out instead of just cheques.
